stories.title: Zebkit – Chromium as an embeddable library
stories.author: Riiiiichard

topComments.author: Riiiiichard
topComments.text: Electron makes your app live inside its runtime. Its windows, its Node, its packaging. I wanted the opposite: Chromium as a library, the way you'd add SQLite. zebkit is Blink, V8, PDFium and FFmpeg in one library you link into your own program, in C, Rust, Python or JavaScript. Your app keeps its own event loop, windows and toolkit. Where it needs the web it adds a view. It can be a window, a child of your own window (X11, NSView, HWND), or off-screen with the frames handed to you. Against the latest Electron (45.2.1), on Linux: - 34% smaller (62 MB compressed) - cold start in 2.3 s instead of 6.6 - pages in 29% less memory - same DOM, text-layout and JavaScript speed No Node: your app is native code, or JavaScript run on the engine's own V8. Everything the engine would show the user or ask of the system is your app's to decide: - permissions, popups, downloads and certificates - network requests, at every stage - the window frame, so the page can be your title bar - menus, dialogs, notifications and tray icons - USB, HID and serial device pickers - screen capture Without your code, a page gets nothing a cautious browser wouldn't give it. For automation and AI agents, it speaks CDP as Chromium's own DevTools server, so Puppeteer, Playwright and any CDP client connect unchanged. It also runs Playwright's API natively inside the engine, with no CDP, no Node and no JSON between processes. A click takes 2 ms instead of 33 ms with Playwright on Chrome over CDP, and a screenshot 12 ms instead of 34. Playwright's own clients can attach to that with chromium.connect(), and there's an MCP server. It also exports Chromium's own C libraries for your app (SQLite, BoringSSL, ICU, HarfBuzz, zstd and others), plus a full PDF API. Chromium 157. Linux, macOS (Apple silicon) and Windows. cargo add zebkit, or pip install zebkit. https://github.com/ikey4u/zebkit I'd love feedback, especially from people who've hit Electron's or CEF's limits.

jobs.text: Those fucking rent-seeking hyperscalers took the internet away from you, and we’re going to give it back to you and to everyone. Broadband brought our parents and grandparents online, but the shift to the non-technical majority created an opportunity to grossly oversimplify everything. Everything dumbed down into a pre-packaged product. Startups began turning their offerings into walled gardens. Platforms took precedence over protocols. APIs and access and data export went away. We’re digesting second-class apps and platforms into first-class applications, libraries, and APIs with full MCP support. We’re distilling out the good parts, and we’re building the connective tissue that draws them together. 100% of the internet is going to be open source soon, and we’re going to force it open. Loudly. We have eight figures in run rate revenue, over 20M app downloads and growing. Our community is the best part, and it’s energetic like a wildfire. Everyone resonates with our mission. We’re missionaries, not mercenaries. We are going to slay the incumbents by being better. Our motto is Google’s old motto - “Don't be evil (tm)”. We’re a tiny team looking for strong engineers to own major parts of the product: desktop apps, lots of completely open source backend infrastructure, agent workflows, agentic app factories. Stack: Rust, a sprinkle of TypeScript/React, egui, Tauri, MySQL/Postgres, Redis, Elasticsearch, Kubernetes. Lots and lots of Rust. We’re systems engineers by trade, but we like to vibe code Rust. Did I say Rust? Rust. Rust Rust Rust. Maybe that's a filter. You have to be self-directed and independent. If you want to open source Salesforce with half your time, do it! If you want to work on Solidworks 3D printing applications, great! Writing music apps and DAWs? Go for it! Custom Discord/Slack clients for our custom, completely open source chat API and platform? Hell yeah. Our organization is flat, and we're going to go after everybody and everything. Everything you build here will be open source. We have no private repos. We can reclaim the internet. That’s our mission. Want to know more about us? Look up “Adobe ArtCraft” on YouTube / TikTok / your platform of choice. If this resonates with you, email hn@storyteller.ai with your Github, a little about yourself and something you’ve built. Write the sentence, “don’t take my RAM, Sam!” so we know you’re one of the good guys.

One document in Mongo is the equivalent of N chunks in Elasticsearch, so in Elasticsearch I do an "update many" (_update_by_query with a filter and a script). Meanwhile, the document in Mongo is deleted, so the two are inconsistent. We do have an application-level lock per document, so the two requests never run at the same time. But this doesn't help here: the second request runs after the first one has finished, and _delete_by_query still searches the last refreshed state, so it sees the old version of the chunks. Have you had a similar problem with Elasticsearch, and how did you solve it? Refreshing on every request is not an option.

I'm curious how commercial GSM gateway manufacturers typically implement communication with their GSM modules. Do they generally use the standard AT command interface provided by the modem manufacturer, or do they develop custom firmware to communicate with the GSM chipset directly, bypassing the AT command layer? For example, do manufacturers of multi-channel GSM VoIP gateways (Dinstar, OpenVox, etc.) communicate with modules using standard AT commands, or do they have some kind of proprietary low-level interface or custom modem firmware? I'd be particularly interested in understanding how they handle voice transmission, call control, and simultaneous operation of multiple GSM channels.

stackOverflowQuestions.title: Databricks Unity Catalog JDBC Connection: Can properties reference Databricks Secrets
stackOverflowQuestions.bodyExcerpt: I'm creating a JDBC connection in Databricks Unity Catalog to connect to Trino. The connection requires SSL configuration, including a client keystore and truststore. When creating the connection through the Databricks UI, I enter these as key-value pairs under the connection's additional options. My concern is that the following properties contain sensitive passwords: SSLKeyStorePassword SSLTrustStorePassword I have two questions: 1. Can I reference Databricks secrets in these JDBC connection properties? For example, is there a supported way to reference a secret scope and key instead of entering the password as a literal value? 2. If secret references are not supported, how are these key-value pairs stored and protected? After creating the Unity Catalog connection through the UI, I can no longer see the original key-value pairs. Are the connection properties, particularly passwords, stored securely by Databricks? Are passwords encrypted at rest? Can users with USE CONNECTION permission retrieve or view these passwords? Is there official Databricks documentation explaining how sensitive JDBC connection properties are stored and protected? I have looked through the Databricks documentation for Unity Catalog JDBC connections, but I haven't found a clear explanation of secret references or the storage and security model for sensitive additional options.

stackOverflowQuestions.title: Should I use space.static_body or create my own static body?
stackOverflowQuestions.bodyExcerpt: I want to create a static body in Pymunk. I've been using pymunk.Body so far: space = pymunk.Space() body = pymunk.Body(body_type=pymunk.Body.STATIC) shape = pymunk.Circle(body, radius=10) space.add(body, shape) But I recently learnt that space has its own static body space.static_body : space = pymunk.Space() shape = pymunk.Circle(space.static_body, radius=10) space.add(shape) From the docs : property static_body: Body A dedicated static body for the space. You don’t have to use it, but many times it can be convenient to have a static body together with the space. Another docs page : Static bodies are bodies that never (or rarely) move. [...] Every space provide [sic] a built-in static body for your convenience. It certainly is very convenient, as I don't need to manually create a static body now. In that case, why do we still have pymunk.Body(body_type=pymunk.Body.STATIC) ? In what situation would I need to create a static body manually?

By Daniel Dominguez
infoqArticles.author: Daniel Dominguez

infoqArticles.title: Cloudflare Develops Public Certificate Authority for Post-Quantum Web Security
infoqArticles.description: Cloudflare is developing a public certificate authority for Merkle Tree Certificates (MTCs) to reduce the bandwidth overhead of post-quantum cryptography. A Chrome experiment served billions of MTCs to 50% of Chrome Beta 146 for selected domains, reporting 9% faster median performance. Wider deployment depends on browser support, transparency, and production-scale validation. By Leela Kumili
infoqArticles.author: Leela Kumili

infoqArticles.title: AWS Launches TorchNeuron to Run PyTorch Models on AWS Trainium Without Modifications
infoqArticles.description: At the recent PyTorch Conference North America 2026, Amazon introduced TorchNeuron, a native PyTorch backend that enables developers to run existing PyTorch code on AWS Trainium AI chips with virtually no code modifications. By Sergio De Simone
infoqArticles.author: Sergio De Simone

infoqArticles.title: Podcast: Distributed LLM Inference on Kubernetes with llm-d, Wasm, & TornadoVM
infoqArticles.description: In this episode, Edoardo Vacchi discusses the evolving landscape of WebAssembly on the backend, running Java workloads on GPUs using TornadoVM, and optimizing distributed AI inference using llm-d and vLLM on Kubernetes. Edoardo explains how llm-d manages cache locality (KV and prefix caches), request routing, and batch inference across Kubernetes clusters to maximize expensive GPU utilization. By
infoqArticles.author: Edoardo Vacchi

infoqArticles.title: Article: Agentic AI Architecture: Current Challenges and Future Opportunities
infoqArticles.description: Agentic AI architecture extends microservices and cloud-native architectures with AI agents that work with context, memory, and protocols such as MCP and A2A. The article covers bounded-context integration, task-dependent coordination strategies, new security risks, and observability needs. It expects gradual adoption alongside existing architectures, with platforms absorbing common components. By
infoqArticles.author: Rafał Gancarz

infoqArticles.title: Pinterest Replaces Journey Clustering with 4B Qwen3 LLM, Reports Improved Engagement

infoqArticles.author: Matt Foster

infoqArticles.title: Tokio Releases Topcoat: A Batteries-Included Full-Stack Rust Framework
infoqArticles.description: Topcoat is an open-source, server-rendered full-stack web framework for Rust from the Tokio team, now public at version 0.9. It uses Rust expressions translated to JavaScript for reactivity instead of WebAssembly. It targets typical database-driven apps. Releases are unstable, and authentication and background jobs remain on the roadmap. By Daniel Curtis
infoqArticles.author: Daniel Curtis

infoqArticles.title: Entire's Git Forge Rethinks Git Collaboration for Coding Agents
infoqArticles.description: Entire is a Git forge designed specifically for collaboration between human developers and AI coding agents. Its premise is that traditional software development infrastructure, particularly the pull request (PR) model, is not well suited to an environment where AI agents generate, review, and iterate on code at high speed. By Sergio De Simone
infoqArticles.author: Sergio De Simone

infoqArticles.title: Google Cloud Adds Self-Managed VMware Cloud Foundation on Bare Metal
infoqArticles.description: Google Cloud has made a self-managed VMware solution generally available, running VMware Cloud Foundation 9.x on dedicated Z3 bare metal with root access across ESXi, vCenter and NSX in 22 regions. It sits beside the Google-managed VMware Engine and matches customer-operated offerings from AWS and Oracle, shifting lifecycle, patching and Broadcom licensing back to the customer. By Steef-Jan Wigger
infoqArticles.author: Steef-Jan Wiggers

infoqArticles.title: Cloudflare Scales D1 Control Plane to Millions of Databases
infoqArticles.description: In a recent article, Cloudflare shared the redesign of the control plane of its D1 serverless SQL database to support millions of databases, avoiding centralized bottlenecks, implementing retries and idempotency, and using eventual consistency. By Renato Losio
infoqArticles.author: Renato Losio

infoqArticles.title: How Grab Improved Mobile App Stability by Safely Handling Surge in AI-Generated Code Changes
infoqArticles.description: The growing adoption of AI coding assistants has accelerated development and increased the volume of code changes per release, bringing more opportunities for defects and crashes, says Grab. To address these challenges, they implemented a layered defense strategy to prevent, detect, and contain crashes throughout the development and release lifecycle. By Sergio De Simone
infoqArticles.author: Sergio De Simone

infoqArticles.title: Open Source pg_vectorsearch Brings More Scalable Vector Search to PostgreSQL
infoqArticles.description: Tiger Data has released pg_vectorsearch, an open source PostgreSQL extension for vector similarity search, currently in alpha. Its PRISM index uses data partitioning and compression instead of the graph-based approach used by pgvector’s HNSW index, reducing memory requirements and index build times. By Renato Losio
infoqArticles.author: Renato Losio

infoqArticles.title: Varlock Releases Bumpy: a File-Based Versioning Alternative to Changesets
infoqArticles.description: Bumpy is an MIT-licensed, TypeScript tool for version management and changelogs in monorepos. It follows the changesets workflow, using markdown bump files, and adds support for workspace and catalog protocols, custom publish commands, and branch-based prereleases. Changesets v3, released in August 2026, closed many earlier gaps, though differences remain. By Daniel Curtis
infoqArticles.author: Daniel Curtis

infoqArticles.title: Yelp Combines Native and Server-Driven UI for its AI Assistant
infoqArticles.description: Yelp combines native mobile controls with server-driven conversation rendering in its AI Assistant using the CHAOS framework. The architecture separates view configuration from conversation data, supports backend-driven chat interactions, and enables faster UI updates without new app releases. Yelp also discusses cross-platform challenges and reuse for its Biz Ask Anything pilot. By Leela Kumili
